leads.name: Quercus sinuata var. breviloba, Texas Big Tree Registry TreeID 543 (Sunset Valley Bigelow/Durand Oak)
leads.reason: Verify pass of 2026-09-27 found a SECOND SOURCE beyond the registry: Sunset Valley's own Public Works and Environmental Services page (fetched via Wayback Machine, 2026-03-09 snapshot, since the live page 403s automated fetches) states in its own words 'Sunset Valley is home to a champion Bigelow Oak (Quercus durandii). There are also several other noteworthy trees in Sunset Valley.' That is a real second source (a small municipality's own environmental department, not the registry) and existence/species is now solid. Girth 124in (3.15m), condition code 3, owner of record City of Sunset Valley, PublicOrPrivate=1 per the registry (measured June 2024, recent). STILL NOT SHIPPED: reverse-geocoding the registry's coordinate (30.21883333, -97.81611111) lands on an unnamed building at 792 Oakdale Drive, Sunset Valley, which is NOT the city hall address (3205 Jones Road) and reads more like a private residential street than a park or municipal site. This does not match the confident 'City of Sunset Valley, PublicOrPrivate=1' ownership tag cleanly, so hard rule 10 access is unresolved rather than confirmed: either the coordinate is imprecise (plausible, this registry's coordinates are not always tree-exact) or the city owns/leases a small parcel or easement on that street that a search could not confirm. Needs: an OSM access-tag check (Overpass was unreachable this pass, HTTP 406) or a direct query to Sunset Valley Public Works, before this can ship even as a register-alone flagged entry. Distance 8.8 km from central Austin; Capital Metro puts Sunset Valley to downtown at roughly 35 minutes by bus, borderline but plausible for the day-trip boundary given Sunset Valley is fully surrounded by and enclaved within Austin.

leads.name: Carya illinoinensis, Texas Big Tree Registry TreeID 10442 (largest pecan in Travis County, Pflugerville)
leads.reason: Verify pass of 2026-09-27: existence/species/age are now well sourced. explorepf.com (Pflugerville's own tourism/explore site) confirms it independently of the registry: 'the largest Pecan tree in Travis County and the 17th largest Pecan tree in the state of Texas,' in Gilleland Creek Park along the Gilleland Creek Trail between the pool and pavilion, 100 North Railroad Avenue, with 'estimates... that this tree is over 300 years old' (a vague age from a real source, keep it vague, never sharpen to a number). Registry gives girth 192in/488cm, height 87ft/26.5m, measured June 2023 (recent), owner City of Pflugerville, PublicOrPrivate=1: existence, species, age and access all check out and this is public parkland. NOT SHIPPED FOR AUSTIN: 23.1 km from central Austin, and this pass checked actual Capital Metro travel time rather than assuming it: the fastest realistic public-transit path (bus to the Howard/Center Line CapMetro Rail stop, then rail to Austin History Center Station) takes at least 34 to 54 minutes door to door, well past the ~30 minute day-trip boundary CLAUDE.md and BRIEF_RESEARCH.md both set, and driving is about 19 minutes but that is not the test. This is the same shape of finding as the already-recorded Kyle Auction Oak: a genuine, well-documented, actively-loved local landmark that is not within Austin's own day-trip boundary by public transport. Stays a lead: worth its own place later (Pflugerville, a real Austin-area city in its own right) or a future 'Austin day trips' collection, not worth quietly stretching Austin's container to include it.

leads.name: Red Bud Isle Cypress (Bald Cypress, 2009 Austin Tree of the Year, Large Tree category)
leads.reason: Found fresh (not from the registry) in the 2026-09-27 verify pass via the Austin Tree of the Year Awards' own naming: the Austin Chronicle's 2012-era roundup of every winner ('Kevin Curtin Hung Out With All of Austin's Tree of the Year Winners') and austin.com's '10 Majestic Austin Trees' both independently describe a bald cypress 'on the southwestern bank' / 'Red Bud peninsula' of Red Bud Isle (3401 Red Bud Trail, a small public City of Austin park/island, address confirmed via OSM) winning the 2009 award. NOT SHIPPED: Red Bud Isle is small but genuinely has many bald cypresses along its banks (47 iNaturalist observations of Taxodium distichum within 500m, several research-grade and recent, spanning the whole shoreline), and neither source pins a single trunk distinctly enough to identify which one won, the way the Sorin Oak's own iNaturalist caption or the Durand Oak's metal tag #809 do. Shipping without that would risk sending a reader to the wrong cypress among several similar ones, which BRIEF_RESEARCH.md's Nigatsu-do lesson warns against directly. No age or girth figure found in either fetched source. Worth a second look if the Austin Heritage Tree Foundation's own award record (rather than a journalist's paraphrase) ever surfaces with a photo or a more specific description ('nearest the boat ramp', 'the one with the double trunk', etc).

leads.name: Kyle Auction Oak
leads.species: Live Oak (Quercus virginiana or Quercus fusiformis, not yet settled)
leads.reason: The town of Kyle was sold off under this oak in 1880: the railroad auctioned the business and most residential lots in its shade and ran free trains from Austin to draw buyers. The county historical commission braced it after it began to split. Downtown Kyle at 204 S. Sledge Street, about 34 km from central Austin, slightly past the 30 km line; decide container before writing. RESOLVED 2026-09-27, verify pass: existence/species/history confirmed by 4 independent sources beyond the finding aid (official Texas Historical Marker #10289 text, Kyle Chamber of Commerce, a 2014 Hays Free Press news story naming the Hays County Historical Commission ecology chairman who had it cross-braced and cabled after a canopy split, and a dated 2019 visitor account with on-site photos and GPS). Species: Live Oak, exact variety not settled by any source. ALIVE: confirmed in 2014 (active professional preservation, named source) and again by a personal visit in 2019; nothing found suggests removal since, and the Chamber still lists it today, but no observation from the last few years exists, so any use should flag that gap. ACCESS: the tree stands on private residential land at 204 S. Sledge Street (a 2019 visitor: "Being on personal property, I did not feel comfortable clawing around"), but the historical marker and the tree itself are in front of the house, viewable and photographable from the public street/sidewalk; a view-only entry (pin at the viewing place, access line stating plainly it stands on private land and is seen from the street) would be honest if this ever ships. CONTAINER, the open question: NOT Austin. No public transport connects Kyle to Austin at all today, so the ~30-minutes-by-public-transport day-trip test cannot be honestly claimed regardless of the 34km driving distance: Capital MetroRail's lines run nowhere near Kyle (the Green Line under construction serves NE Austin/Colony Park, unrelated direction); the Lone Star Rail District commuter-rail plan for the Austin-Kyle-San Marcos-San Antonio corridor died in 2016 when Union Pacific withdrew, and a 2024 revival push has produced no service; CARTS, the regional rural transit agency, explicitly does not serve Kyle as an urbanized-area stop (only a once-a-week Country Bus route touches Kyle from Dripping Springs/Wimberley). NOT its own place either, on balance: this is a well-loved, actively-preserved local landmark with a genuine town-founding story and an official state historical marker, but nothing found suggests people travel to Kyle specifically for this one tree the way they would for an Angel Oak or a Bartram's Ginkgo, so it likely does not clear the single-famous-tree exception (2026-08-31) on its own. Stays a lead: worth a look again if Kyle ever accumulates enough separately-verified trees to reach its own four-tree floor, or if a future "day trips" collection wants a well-documented outlier.
sources: https://texashistoricalmarkers.weebly.com/kyle-auction-oak.html (quotes official Texas Historical Marker No. 10289 text in full)
https://www.kylechamber.org/historical-sites (Kyle Area Chamber of Commerce, current official listing)
https://www.carolynhestand.com/blog/kyle-auction-oak (dated visitor account, 2019-10-20, with photo and on-site GPS)

blocked.name: Quercus sinuata var. breviloba, Texas Big Tree Registry TreeID 970
sources: Texas Big Tree Registry, Texas A&M Forest Service (texasforestinfo.tamu.edu/BigTreeRegistry). Non-commercial licence: usable as a lead and verification source, never imported. See OPEN_DATA_SURVEY.md.
blocked.why_blocked: PRIVATE LAND. The Texas Big Tree Registry's PublicOrPrivate flag is 0 on this tree, and the flag is not the undocumented mystery an earlier pass took it for: across all 660 swept trees, flag 1 belongs to Big Bend and Guadalupe Mountains National Parks, Sam Houston National Forest, state natural areas and TxDOT districts, while flag 0 belongs to Big Tree Ranch, X-Arrow Ranch, Little Sandy Hunting & Fishing Club and similar. It means what it says. The registry also sets Display 0 on almost all of them, so it withholds these locations from its own public map, and hard rule 10 is absolute about not undoing that: the coordinates only reached us because the backend returns what the front end hides. Never ship unless a source shows the site is genuinely open to visitors.

notes.note: Swept from the corrected Texas Big Tree Registry pull (scripts/texas_big_trees.py). Circumference is INCHES: an earlier Houston pass read it as centimetres and concluded the state was thin. Coordinates decide which city a tree belongs to, never CountyName.

PublicOrPrivate decoded from the data itself: flag 1 is national parks, national forests, state natural areas and TxDOT; flag 0 is ranches and hunting clubs. Flag 0 trees moved to blocked under hard rule 10, since the registry also hides them from its own public map and their coordinates only reached us because the backend returns what the front end withholds. OrganizationName names the owner and is the field a verify pass should lead with.

Deepen verify pass (US-priority). Shipped 4 trees to data/research/austin-verified.json: the Littlefield Cedar (Cedrus deodara, TreeID 1046, UT Austin campus), the Durand Oak of Sir Swante Palm Park (Quercus sinuata var. sinuata, TreeID 1111, Waller Creek Greenbelt), the Sorin Oak (Quercus fusiformis, St. Edward's University, found fresh via the Austin Tree of the Year Awards rather than the registry), and the Mother Pecan (Carya illinoinensis, Zilker Park, also found via the Tree of the Year Awards). Both Littlefield Cedar and Sir Swante Palm's Durand Oak leads (TreeIDs 1046 and 1111) are removed from this file's leads list since they are now published data, not open leads. Moved to blocked: Ilex decidua TreeID 15446 (private HOA land), Chilopsis linearis TreeID 32449 (private, Display 0, and 26.8km out), Rhus virens TreeID 887 (private community, Display 0, and 27.6km out) -- all three confirmed via direct query of the full registry attribute set (PublicOrPrivate, Display, OrganizationName), which is more reliable than the coordinate-only leads this file used to carry. Also removed stale duplicate lead entries for TreeID 970, 6435, 29446, 1077 and 29445, which were already correctly present in the blocked list under identical coordinates; the leads list should not carry a second, weaker copy of an entry already blocked. Carya illinoinensis TreeID 10442 (Pflugerville) and Quercus sinuata var. breviloba TreeID 543 (Sunset Valley) got real second sources this pass (a city tourism page and a municipal environmental-services page respectively) but were NOT shipped: Pflugerville's transit time to central Austin measured at 34-54 minutes, past the day-trip boundary, the same problem as the already-recorded Kyle Auction Oak; Sunset Valley's registry coordinate reverse-geocodes to a residential-looking address that does not match its own city hall, so hard rule 10 access needs a further check before it can ship even flagged as register-plus-one-source. New lead added: the Red Bud Isle Cypress (2009 Tree of the Year), held back only because Red Bud Isle has many similar bald cypresses and no source pins which specific trunk won. The Austin Tree of the Year Awards / Austin Heritage Tree Foundation is confirmed as a real naming body for this city (per BRIEF_RESEARCH.md's 'does anybody name its trees' rule) and is worth checking again for future passes: austintreeoftheyearawards.org/winners-gallery 404s directly but the Austin Chronicle's own roundup of every winner through 2012 and austin.com's tree listicle both reproduce entries from it.
